content.title: He stole a plane from Sea-Tac and then crashed it. She wanted to know why
content.text: AUSTIN, Texas — It’s a sweltering day at the 2026 SXSW Film & TV Festival, and director Patricia E. Gillespie has just finished taking part in a true crime panel. She’s there with her new Hulu documentary, “#SkyKing,” which explores the life and death of Richard “Beebo” Russell, a 28-year-old Horizon Air ground service agent who, in 2018, stole a plane from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, flew it for more than an hour, performed a barrel roll and crashed on Ketron Island. The incident made headlines around the world, and Russell posthumously became a person of immense interest to many online (hence the “hashtag” in the film’s title).For Gillespie, who has previously worked in the true crime genre, there was more to this story that she wanted to explore, even if she doesn’t think her new film fits neatly into that category. “I’ve never made whodunits, I’ve tried to make why-it’d-happens,” said Gillespie, who got her start in features working as a script supervisor on the revenge thriller “Blue Ruin” before becoming a producer and director on documentaries like “Whose Streets?” and “The Secrets We Bury.” “I’ve always worked near this medium, but I don’t view this as purely a true crime film. … Crime-adjacent storytelling will always have a place in my heart, but I think there are many different kinds of important stories, and I think this touches a lot of the buckets. I think this is a class story, I think it’s a story about men and mental health.”The “why’d it happen” of “#SkyKing” centers on not just the actual audio from Russell speaking directly to air traffic control that gets edited together with re-creations, but extended interviews with family members as they listen to him and reflect on his life. It was these people who Gillespie said she wanted to, more than anything, do right by with her film. This included his mother, Karen, who Gillespie said surprised her by deciding to watch the world premiere at SXSW. “It was really special to see it with Karen,” Gillespie said. “You make your film for a big audience, but there is often a person that you make the film for. As much as we made this film for Beebo and people like him, Karen just stole all of our hearts. We made it … not knowing if she’d ever want to see it, so it was really special for her to see her in there and be next to her and watch her watch it.” Another group Gillespie thought of while making her film? Those who connected with the story online, cutting the footage of Russell flying and his statements into tribute videos that often use the M83 songs “My Tears Are Becoming a Sea” and “Outro.” Gillespie uses the latter in the film when Russell successfully does a barrel roll shortly before crashing. “This was something that existed on the internet that moved a lot of people that went viral. We wanted to tip our hat to that and that was the song that was largely associated with (the barrel roll) on TikTok,” Gillespie said. “What a great song, it’s in so many movies. … I thought it was beautiful that this grandiose piece of music that’s often associated with these big, hero moments was applied to this guy. There was something about it that I found moving. ” Related While Gillespie said she wanted to make sure not to lose sight of the people at the center, focusing more on Russell’s family and those who knew him over the broader political conversations that came up surrounding the incident, there was still divisive discourse online that the “#Skyking” director wanted to address.“When you see what went on online, it got so polarized and everybody wanted to make him the poster boy of whatever their thing was at the moment. It was clear that a lot of the story was missing, and so I saw my job as trying to figure out what piece of that story we’re missing,” Gillespie said. “It’s very much about trying to take that out of the immediately political and put it into the personalized experience to fill in those details,” Gillespie said. “It was such a hard moment because the country was facing a lot. It wasn’t that far from the awful stuff that happened in Charlottesville. It was just a very tense time and some of his comments were indeed inflammatory, but I saw major news publications cut out the inflammatory lines rather than try to explain them or see where they came from. There is a lack of curiosity that keeps us from talking.”The film also addresses how Russell was claimed by white supremacist groups following one comment he made about how he wouldn’t get a job as a pilot even if he landed the plane because he was “a white guy.” In the film, family members said this statement was ultimately misconstrued and denounced the hate groups as not reflecting who Russell was or his beliefs.“His family wanted to take that legacy back because it wasn’t something he would stand by, and I think they’ve successfully done that. I think it’s going to be hard to sell a T-shirt for your white nationalist agenda of this guy if enough people watch the movie, and that I feel really proud of,” Gillespie said. “Beyond that, I can’t control how people take it, but I hope people approach it with open ears and open hearts.” The film, which was shot at the airport and in the state, puts itself in dialogue with other local voices. At one point, as Gillespie’s subjects discuss the response to Russell’s theft of the plane, the film briefly cuts to a column written by Charles Mudede in The Stranger. Mudede is also making his own documentary about the incident with fellow Seattle filmmaker Robinson Devor.“I heard about it recently and, actually, I’m super interested to see their film,” Gillespie said. “I loved (Robinson’s) ‘Zoo,’ I love that film, so I’m sure they have a different take. I’m sure it’s going to be great.” ‘#SkyKing’ The film is available to stream on Hulu starting April 14.
